The agent generates SQL based on the user's natural language question, calls the Lambda function, and uses the results to formulate a response. Fine-tuning (option A) can improve SQL generation but requires retraining when the schema changes. Storing the entire database in context (option C) is not feasible for large databases and would consume the entire context window. Using Athena directly (option D) requires users to write SQL, which defeats the purpose of natural language querying.

questions.question: A company is implementing a RAG system and wants to evaluate whether their retrieval component is finding the relevant documents. They measure the percentage of relevant documents that were retrieved out of all relevant documents in the corpus. Which metric are they measuring?
options: Precision — the percentage of retrieved documents that are relevant
Accuracy — the percentage of all documents correctly classified as relevant or irrelevant
Recall — the percentage of all relevant documents in the corpus that were successfully retrieved
F1 score — the harmonic mean of precision and recall for retrieval
questions.explanation: Recall is correct — it measures what fraction of all relevant documents were retrieved. Recall = (relevant documents retrieved) / (total relevant documents in corpus). High recall means the retrieval system finds most of the relevant documents. Precision (option A) measures what fraction of retrieved documents are relevant — it answers 'of what I retrieved, how much was useful?' Accuracy (option B) is a classification metric measuring overall correct predictions, not typically used for retrieval evaluation. F1 score (option D) combines precision and recall but the question specifically asks about the metric measuring coverage of relevant documents, which is recall.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Comprehend to analyze customer feedback. They want to automatically categorize feedback into topics (product quality, shipping, customer service) without manually labeling training data. Which Amazon Comprehend feature supports this?
options: Amazon Comprehend Sentiment Analysis to determine if feedback is positive or negative
Amazon Comprehend Topic Modeling to automatically discover topics in a collection of documents without labeled training data
Amazon Comprehend Custom Classification to train a custom classifier on labeled feedback examples
Amazon Comprehend Entity Recognition to extract product names and service types from feedback
questions.explanation: Amazon Comprehend Topic Modeling is correct — it uses unsupervised machine learning (LDA - Latent Dirichlet Allocation) to automatically discover topics in a collection of documents without requiring labeled training data. It identifies clusters of related terms and assigns documents to topics. Sentiment Analysis (option A) determines positive/negative/neutral sentiment but does not categorize by topic. Custom Classification (option C) trains a classifier on labeled examples — the question specifies no manual labeling. Entity Recognition (option D) extracts named entities (people, places, organizations) but does not categorize documents by topic.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Polly to convert text articles to audio for their podcast application. They want the audio to sound natural with appropriate pauses and emphasis. Which Amazon Polly feature provides the most natural-sounding speech?
options: Standard voices using concatenative synthesis for fast, cost-effective audio generation
Neural voices using deep learning to produce more natural-sounding speech with better prosody
SSML (Speech Synthesis Markup Language) tags to manually control every aspect of speech
Long-form voices optimized for reading lengthy documents with consistent quality
questions.explanation: Amazon Polly Neural voices use deep learning (neural TTS) to produce significantly more natural-sounding speech with better prosody, intonation, and rhythm compared to standard voices. They are the recommended choice for applications where audio quality matters. Standard voices (option A) use older concatenative synthesis — faster and cheaper but less natural. SSML (option C) provides fine-grained control over speech but requires manual markup of every article, which is not practical for automated podcast generation. Long-form voices (option D) are optimized for lengthy content but are a subset of neural voices — neural voices are the broader category.

questions.question: A company is building a multi-agent system using Amazon Bedrock where a supervisor agent coordinates multiple specialized sub-agents (research agent, writing agent, review agent). Which Amazon Bedrock Agents feature enables this multi-agent collaboration?
options: Amazon Bedrock Flows to define a fixed workflow connecting the agents
Amazon Bedrock Agents inline agents for lightweight, single-session agent execution
Amazon Bedrock Agents multi-agent collaboration, where a supervisor agent can invoke other agents as sub-agents
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases shared across all agents for common information access
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Agents multi-agent collaboration is correct — it allows a supervisor agent to invoke other Bedrock Agents as sub-agents within an action group. The supervisor agent orchestrates the workflow, delegating tasks to specialized sub-agents and aggregating their results. Bedrock Flows (option A) defines fixed workflows but does not support dynamic agent-to-agent delegation. Inline agents (option B) are lightweight agents for single-session use without persistent configuration — not for multi-agent orchestration. Shared Knowledge Bases (option C) provide common information access but do not enable agent-to-agent coordination.

questions.question: A company wants to use Amazon Translate to automatically translate customer support tickets from 10 different languages into English for their support team. Which Amazon Translate feature allows them to process a large batch of tickets stored in S3 without making individual API calls for each ticket?
options: Amazon Translate real-time translation API called in a loop for each ticket
Amazon Translate Active Custom Translation to improve translation quality for domain-specific terms
Amazon Translate asynchronous batch translation job that processes files from S3 and writes results to S3
Amazon Comprehend language detection followed by Amazon Translate for each detected language
questions.explanation: Amazon Translate asynchronous batch translation is correct — it processes large volumes of documents stored in S3 without individual API calls. You specify the source S3 location, target S3 location, source and target languages, and submit a batch job. Results are written back to S3 when complete. Real-time API in a loop (option A) would work but is inefficient for large batches and does not leverage the batch processing optimization. Active Custom Translation (option B) improves translation quality for domain-specific terminology but is not a batch processing feature. Comprehend + Translate (option C) is a valid pattern for auto-detecting language but adds complexity — Translate batch jobs support automatic language detection.

questions.question: A developer is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a solution where the model generates a structured JSON response (with specific fields like 'sentiment', 'category', 'confidence') instead of free-form text. Which technique ensures structured output?
options: Set temperature to 0 to make the model output deterministic JSON
Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce JSON output format
Specify the required JSON schema in the prompt and use few-shot examples showing the expected format, or use the model's native structured output feature
Post-process the model's text output with a JSON parser and retry if parsing fails
questions.explanation: Specifying the JSON schema in the prompt with few-shot examples (or using native structured output) is the most reliable approach. Modern foundation models can reliably generate structured JSON when given a clear schema and examples. Some models (like Claude) support native structured output modes. Temperature 0 (option A) makes output deterministic but does not guarantee JSON format. Guardrails (option B) apply content safety filters, not output format enforcement. Post-processing with retry (option C) is a fallback strategy but is not the primary technique — it adds latency and complexity.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and wants to implement metadata filtering to restrict retrieval to documents from a specific department or date range. How does metadata filtering work in Bedrock Knowledge Bases?
options: Metadata filtering uses the foundation model to classify documents by department before retrieval
Metadata filtering applies filters on document metadata attributes (stored alongside embeddings in the vector store) to narrow the search space before or after vector similarity search
Metadata filtering requires a separate Amazon DynamoDB table to store document metadata
Metadata filtering is only available when using Amazon OpenSearch Service as the vector store
questions.explanation: Metadata filtering in Bedrock Knowledge Bases applies filters on metadata attributes stored alongside document embeddings in the vector store. When ingesting documents, you can attach metadata (e.g., department, date, document type). At query time, you specify filter conditions (e.g., department = 'Finance' AND date > '2024-01-01') that narrow the search space before or after vector similarity search. The foundation model is not used for filtering (option A) — it is a database-level operation. A separate DynamoDB table (option C) is not required — metadata is stored in the vector store. Metadata filtering is available across multiple vector store backends (option D), not just OpenSearch.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a solution where users can upload images and ask questions about them (e.g., 'What is wrong with this product?' for a photo of a defective item). Which foundation model capability is required?
options: Text-to-image generation to create reference images for comparison
Image segmentation to identify defective regions in the product photo
Multimodal understanding — the model must accept both image and text inputs to answer questions about images
Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels to detect defects in product images
questions.explanation: Multimodal understanding is required — the model must accept both image and text inputs simultaneously to answer questions about the image content. Models like Claude 3 (Haiku, Sonnet, Opus), Amazon Nova Lite/Pro, and others in Bedrock support this. Text-to-image generation (option A) creates images from text, not the reverse. Image segmentation (option B) identifies regions in images but does not answer natural language questions about them. Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels (option C) detects specific objects or defects but requires training data and does not support open-ended natural language questions about arbitrary images.

questions.question: A company wants to use Amazon Q Developer to help their software development team. Which of the following is a primary capability of Amazon Q Developer?
options: Generating business intelligence reports from company data
Answering questions about AWS services and generating, explaining, and debugging code in the IDE
Managing AWS infrastructure deployments and CloudFormation stacks
Analyzing customer sentiment from support tickets
questions.explanation: Amazon Q Developer is correct — it is an AI coding assistant that helps developers by generating code, explaining existing code, debugging, suggesting fixes, and answering questions about AWS services directly in the IDE (VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) and AWS Console. It also supports security vulnerability scanning. Generating BI reports (option A) is Amazon Q in QuickSight. Managing infrastructure deployments (option C) is not a primary Q Developer capability — it focuses on code assistance. Analyzing customer sentiment (option D) is Amazon Comprehend's domain.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a solution where the model can answer questions about documents that are too long to fit in the context window. The documents are stored in S3. Which approach should be used?
options: Summarize each document first, then include all summaries in the context window
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to chunk, embed, and index the documents in a vector store, then retrieve relevant chunks at query time
Split documents into fixed-size chunks and include all chunks in the context window
Use a model with a larger context window that can fit the entire document
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with RAG is the correct approach for documents too long for the context window. Documents are chunked, embedded, and stored in a vector store. At query time, only the most relevant chunks are retrieved and included in the context, making it feasible to query any size document corpus. Summarizing documents (option A) loses detail and may miss specific information needed to answer questions. Including all chunks in context (option C) defeats the purpose if documents are too long. Using a larger context window (option D) helps but has limits — very large document corpora still exceed even the largest context windows, and larger contexts increase cost and latency.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock Agents and wants to implement a code interpreter capability where the agent can write and execute Python code to perform data analysis and return results. Which Amazon Bedrock Agents feature provides this?
options: An action group with a Lambda function that executes Python code submitted by the agent
Amazon Bedrock Agents code interpretation feature, which provides a sandboxed Python execution environment
Amazon SageMaker notebooks integrated with Bedrock Agents for code execution
Amazon Bedrock Flows with a code execution node for running Python scripts
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Agents code interpretation is correct — it provides a built-in sandboxed Python execution environment that the agent can use to write and run code for data analysis, calculations, and file processing. The agent generates Python code, executes it in the sandbox, and uses the output to formulate responses. A Lambda function action group (option A) is a valid alternative but requires the developer to build and maintain the execution infrastructure. SageMaker notebooks (option C) are not integrated with Bedrock Agents for code execution. Bedrock Flows (option D) does not have a code execution node — it orchestrates model invocations and conditions.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a solution where the model generates a response and then automatically evaluates whether the response meets quality criteria (relevance, completeness, accuracy) before returning it to the user. Which pattern implements this?
options: Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to evaluate response quality before returning it
Use a second foundation model call as a judge to evaluate the first model's response against defined criteria
Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to evaluate response quality in production
Use Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to assess response quality in real time
questions.explanation: Using a second model as a judge (LLM-as-a-judge) is correct for automated quality evaluation. After the primary model generates a response, a second model call evaluates it against defined criteria (relevance, completeness, accuracy) and returns a score or pass/fail. If the response fails, it can be regenerated or flagged. Guardrails (option A) apply content safety filters (harmful content, PII, topics) but do not evaluate quality criteria like relevance or completeness. SageMaker Model Monitor (option C) monitors deployed models for drift in production, not real-time response quality. Bedrock Model Evaluation (option D) runs batch evaluations, not real-time per-response evaluation.

questions.question: A company wants to use Amazon Transcribe to transcribe customer service calls and automatically identify which parts of the conversation were spoken by the customer versus the agent. Which Amazon Transcribe feature provides this?
options: Amazon Transcribe custom vocabulary to improve recognition of company-specific terms
Amazon Transcribe speaker diarization (speaker identification) to label each speech segment with a speaker ID
Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics to analyze call sentiment and identify speakers in contact center calls
Amazon Transcribe custom language models to improve accuracy for the specific domain
questions.explanation: Amazon Transcribe Call Analytics is correct for contact center use cases — it is specifically designed for customer service calls and provides speaker identification (customer vs. agent), sentiment analysis per speaker, call characteristics (interruptions, talk time), and issue detection. Speaker diarization (option B) labels speakers as 'Speaker 1', 'Speaker 2' etc. but does not specifically identify customer vs. agent roles. Custom vocabulary (option A) improves recognition of specific terms but does not identify speakers. Custom language models (option D) improve accuracy for domain-specific language but do not identify speakers.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a solution where the model can access real-time information from the web to answer questions about current events. Which approach should be used?
options: Use a foundation model with a very recent training cutoff date to minimize knowledge gaps
Implement a web search tool using Amazon Bedrock Agents tool use, where the agent calls a web search API and incorporates the results into its response
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with a web crawler data source that indexes public websites
Fine-tune the foundation model weekly on recent news articles to keep it current
questions.explanation: Bedrock Agents with a web search tool is correct for real-time web access. The agent is configured with a tool that calls a web search API (e.g., Bing Search, Google Custom Search). When a user asks about current events, the agent calls the search tool, retrieves current results, and incorporates them into the response. Recent training cutoff (option A) reduces but does not eliminate knowledge gaps — models cannot know events after their cutoff. Knowledge Bases with web crawler (option C) indexes websites periodically but is not real-time — there is a delay between web changes and index updates. Weekly fine-tuning (option D) is expensive, time-consuming, and still not real-time.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a solution where the model generates a response and then automatically checks whether the response contains any personally identifiable information (PII) before returning it to the user. Which Amazon Bedrock feature provides this PII detection and masking?
options: Amazon Macie to scan model responses for PII in S3
Amazon Comprehend PII detection applied to model responses as a post-processing step
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with sensitive information filters configured to detect and mask PII in model inputs and outputs
AWS Lambda function to scan responses for PII patterns using regex before returning them
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with sensitive information filters is correct — it is natively integrated with Bedrock and can detect and mask PII (names, email addresses, phone numbers, SSNs, credit card numbers, etc.) in both model inputs and outputs in real time. It can be configured to block, mask, or anonymize PII. Amazon Macie (option A) scans S3 for PII in stored data, not real-time model responses. Amazon Comprehend PII detection (option B) is a valid approach but requires a separate API call and custom integration. Lambda with regex (option C) can detect simple patterns but misses complex PII and requires maintenance.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a solution where the model can answer questions about their internal APIs by reading the OpenAPI specification. The model should be able to explain endpoints, parameters, and response formats. Which approach provides the best results?
options: Fine-tune the foundation model on the OpenAPI specification to embed API knowledge in the model weights
Include the entire OpenAPI specification in the system prompt for every request
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases to index the OpenAPI specification and retrieve relevant sections based on the user's question
Use Amazon Bedrock Agents with the OpenAPI specification as an action group schema, allowing the model to understand and call the APIs
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with the OpenAPI specification indexed is correct for answering questions about API documentation. The specification is chunked and indexed, and relevant sections (specific endpoints, parameters) are retrieved based on the user's question. This handles large specifications that may not fit in the context window. Fine-tuning (option A) embeds knowledge in weights but requires retraining when the API changes. Including the entire spec in the system prompt (option B) works for small specs but large OpenAPI specs can exceed context window limits. Bedrock Agents with the spec as an action group (option C) enables the model to call the APIs, not just answer questions about them — a different use case.

questions.question: A company is deploying an AI model that makes loan approval decisions. Regulators require that applicants be able to understand why their application was approved or denied. Which approach provides the most actionable explanation for individual predictions?
options: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values, which quantify each feature's contribution to a specific prediction
Model accuracy metrics (precision, recall, F1) to demonstrate overall model fairness
A confusion matrix showing the model's performance across different demographic groups
Feature importance scores showing which features are most important globally across all predictions
questions.explanation: SHAP values are correct for individual prediction explanations. SHAP assigns each feature a contribution value for a specific prediction, showing how much each feature pushed the prediction toward approval or denial. This provides actionable, instance-level explanations (e.g., 'Your application was denied primarily because of your debt-to-income ratio'). Model accuracy metrics (option B) describe overall performance, not individual decisions. A confusion matrix (option C) shows aggregate performance across groups but not individual explanations. Global feature importance (option D) shows which features matter most on average but does not explain individual predictions.

questions.question: A company is training a machine learning model for hiring decisions and discovers that the training data reflects historical hiring patterns where certain demographic groups were underrepresented. What is the most appropriate action to address this bias?
options: Remove demographic features (age, gender, ethnicity) from the training data to prevent the model from using them
Collect additional training data that better represents underrepresented groups, and use techniques like re-weighting or re-sampling to balance the dataset
Accept the bias as a reflection of historical reality and document it in the model card
Deploy the model and monitor for bias in production using SageMaker Model Monitor
questions.explanation: Collecting representative data and balancing the dataset is the most appropriate action. Addressing bias at the data level is more effective than post-hoc fixes. Re-weighting gives more importance to underrepresented examples; re-sampling (oversampling minority groups or undersampling majority groups) balances the distribution. Removing demographic features (option A) does not eliminate bias — the model can learn proxies for demographic attributes from other correlated features (proxy discrimination). Accepting bias (option C) is not responsible AI practice. Monitoring in production (option D) detects bias after deployment but does not address the root cause — bias should be addressed before deployment.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon SageMaker Clarify to analyze their model for bias. They want to measure whether the model's positive prediction rate differs significantly between demographic groups. Which bias metric measures this?
options: Class Imbalance (CI) — measures the imbalance in the number of samples between groups in the training data
Disparate Impact (DI) — measures the ratio of positive prediction rates between the advantaged and disadvantaged groups
Accuracy Difference — measures the difference in model accuracy between demographic groups
Label Imbalance — measures the difference in positive label rates between groups in the training data
questions.explanation: Disparate Impact (DI) is correct — it measures the ratio of the positive prediction rate for the disadvantaged group to the positive prediction rate for the advantaged group. A DI of 1.0 indicates equal positive prediction rates; values significantly below 1.0 indicate the model predicts positive outcomes less often for the disadvantaged group. This is a key fairness metric in employment and lending contexts. Class Imbalance (option A) measures data imbalance, not prediction rate differences. Accuracy Difference (option C) measures overall accuracy differences, not specifically positive prediction rates. Label Imbalance (option D) measures training data label distribution, not model predictions.

questions.question: A company is deploying a generative AI application and wants to implement human oversight for high-stakes decisions. The AI generates recommendations, but a human must review and approve them before they are acted upon. Which AWS service supports this human-in-the-loop workflow?
options: Amazon SageMaker Clarify to automatically approve or reject AI recommendations
Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to orchestrate the review workflow
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to block recommendations that require human review
Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I) to route AI predictions to human reviewers when confidence is low or for random audits
questions.explanation: Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) is correct for human-in-the-loop workflows. A2I routes AI predictions to human reviewers through a workforce (Amazon Mechanical Turk, private workforce, or vendor workforce) when the model's confidence is below a threshold or for random audits. Reviewers see the AI's prediction and can approve, reject, or correct it. SageMaker Clarify (option A) analyzes bias and explainability but does not route predictions to human reviewers. SageMaker Pipelines (option B) orchestrates ML workflows but is not designed for human review routing. Bedrock Guardrails (option C) applies automated content filters, not human review workflows.

questions.question: A company is documenting their machine learning model for transparency and accountability. They want to create a standardized document that describes the model's intended use, performance metrics, evaluation results, limitations, and ethical considerations. Which AWS tool supports creating this documentation?
options: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards, which provide a structured framework for documenting model details, intended use, performance, and limitations
AWS CloudTrail to log all model training and inference activities
Amazon SageMaker Experiments to track model training runs and metrics
AWS Audit Manager to create compliance reports for the model
questions.explanation: Amazon SageMaker Model Cards is correct — they provide a standardized framework for documenting ML models including intended use cases, training details, evaluation results across different groups, limitations, ethical considerations, and deployment recommendations. Model Cards support transparency and accountability. CloudTrail (option B) logs API calls for audit purposes but does not document model characteristics. SageMaker Experiments (option C) tracks training runs and metrics but is a development tool, not a documentation framework. AWS Audit Manager (option D) creates compliance reports for regulatory frameworks but is not specifically designed for ML model documentation.

questions.question: A company is using a generative AI model for content generation and is concerned about the model producing content that infringes on copyrighted material. Which responsible AI consideration addresses this risk?
options: Configure Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to block all creative content generation
Use only open-source foundation models to avoid copyright concerns
Implement output filtering to detect and block verbatim reproduction of copyrighted text, and review the model's training data provenance and licensing
Require users to sign a terms of service agreement accepting responsibility for copyright compliance
questions.explanation: Output filtering combined with training data provenance review is the most comprehensive approach. Filtering detects verbatim reproduction of copyrighted text in outputs. Reviewing training data provenance ensures the model was trained on appropriately licensed data. This addresses both the output risk and the root cause. Blocking all creative content (option A) is overly restrictive and defeats the purpose of the application. Open-source models (option B) may still have copyright issues depending on their training data. User terms of service (option D) shifts legal responsibility but does not technically prevent copyright infringement — the company may still face liability.

questions.question: A company is evaluating the environmental impact of their AI workloads. They want to choose foundation models that minimize carbon footprint. Which factor most directly affects the carbon footprint of using a foundation model via an API?
options: The geographic region of the API endpoint — regions with renewable energy have lower carbon intensity
The model's parameter count — larger models always have higher carbon footprint per inference
The number of API calls made — more calls always result in higher carbon footprint
The model's training data size — models trained on more data have higher embodied carbon
questions.explanation: The geographic region is the most directly actionable factor for carbon footprint when using a managed API. AWS regions powered by renewable energy (e.g., regions with high renewable energy percentage) have significantly lower carbon intensity per compute unit. Choosing a region with renewable energy can reduce carbon footprint by 80-90% compared to fossil fuel-powered regions. Parameter count (option B) affects compute per inference but smaller models are not always lower carbon — efficiency varies. Number of API calls (option C) affects total carbon but is determined by the application's needs, not a choice. Training data size (option D) affects the model's embodied carbon from training, which is a one-time cost amortized across all inferences.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to prevent users from asking the model questions about competitor products. They want this restriction to apply across all applications using their Bedrock deployment. Which Amazon Bedrock feature implements this topic restriction?
options: A system prompt in each application instructing the model not to discuss competitors
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails with a denied topics configuration that blocks queries about competitor products
IAM policies restricting which users can invoke the Bedrock API
Amazon Bedrock Agents with a routing rule that rejects competitor-related queries
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails denied topics is correct — it allows you to define topics that the model should not engage with (e.g., 'competitor products'). When a user query or model response touches on a denied topic, Guardrails blocks it and returns a configured message. This applies consistently across all applications that use the guardrail. A system prompt (option A) can be bypassed by users who craft adversarial prompts and must be added to each application separately. IAM policies (option C) control API access, not conversation content. Bedrock Agents routing rules (option D) do not exist as a content filtering mechanism.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to log all model invocations (inputs and outputs) for compliance auditing. They need to store these logs in S3 for 7 years. Which Amazon Bedrock feature enables this logging?
options: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging, which captures all API requests and responses and delivers them to CloudWatch Logs or S3
AWS CloudTrail to log all Bedrock API calls including the full request and response payloads
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails audit logging to capture all guardrail evaluations
VPC Flow Logs to capture network traffic to and from the Bedrock API endpoint
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging is correct — it captures the full input prompts and output responses for all model invocations and delivers them to CloudWatch Logs or S3. This is specifically designed for compliance logging of AI interactions. S3 lifecycle policies can retain logs for 7 years. CloudTrail (option B) logs API calls (metadata like who called the API, when, from where) but does not capture the full prompt and response content. Guardrails audit logging (option C) captures guardrail evaluation results but not all invocations. VPC Flow Logs (option D) capture network metadata, not application-level content.

questions.question: A company is implementing IAM policies for Amazon Bedrock. They want to allow a specific application role to invoke only the Claude Sonnet model and no other models. Which IAM policy element restricts access to a specific model?
options: A Condition element using aws:RequestedRegion to restrict to regions where Claude Sonnet is available
A Resource element specifying the ARN of the Claude Sonnet model (arn:aws:bedrock:region::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-3-sonnet-20240229-v1:0)
A Principal element specifying the Claude Sonnet model ARN
A NotAction element listing all other models to deny access
questions.explanation: The Resource element with the specific model ARN is correct for restricting Bedrock access to a specific model. IAM policies for Bedrock use the model ARN as the resource, allowing fine-grained control over which models a role can invoke. The ARN format is arn:aws:bedrock:region::foundation-model/model-id. aws:RequestedRegion condition (option A) restricts by region, not by model. The Principal element (option C) specifies who the policy applies to, not what resources they can access. NotAction (option D) is a valid approach but is more complex and error-prone than explicitly specifying the allowed resource.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and is concerned about prompt injection attacks where malicious content in retrieved documents could override the system prompt and manipulate the model's behavior. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails feature helps mitigate this risk?
options: Content filters to block harmful content in model outputs
Denied topics to prevent the model from discussing sensitive subjects
Contextual grounding checks to verify responses are grounded in source documents
Sensitive information filters to detect and block PII in inputs and outputs
questions.explanation: Contextual grounding checks help mitigate prompt injection by verifying that the model's response is grounded in the provided source documents and does not deviate from the intended context. If injected instructions in retrieved documents cause the model to generate responses not grounded in the legitimate sources, the grounding check can detect and block this. Content filters (option A) block harmful content categories but do not specifically detect prompt injection. Denied topics (option B) block specific topics but do not detect injection attacks. Sensitive information filters (option D) detect PII but do not address prompt injection.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases and wants to ensure that the training data used to build their RAG system is encrypted at rest. Which encryption option is available for data stored in Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases?
options: Data in Knowledge Bases is always encrypted with AWS-managed keys and cannot be changed
Data in Knowledge Bases can be encrypted with AWS-managed keys (default) or customer-managed KMS keys for additional control
Data in Knowledge Bases is not encrypted by default and must be manually encrypted before ingestion
Encryption is only available for the vector store, not for the source documents in S3
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports encryption with both AWS-managed keys (default) and customer-managed KMS keys. Customer-managed keys provide additional control, including the ability to audit key usage, rotate keys, and revoke access. Data is encrypted at rest in both the vector store and the associated S3 storage. The default is AWS-managed keys (option A is partially correct but incomplete — customer-managed keys are also available). Data is not unencrypted by default (option C). Encryption applies to both the vector store and source documents (option D is incorrect).

questions.question: A company wants to ensure their AI system complies with data residency requirements that prohibit customer data from leaving a specific AWS region. Which approach ensures data residency compliance when using Amazon Bedrock?
options: Enable cross-region inference to distribute requests across multiple regions for redundancy
Use Amazon Bedrock in the specific required region and disable cross-region inference to ensure all data processing stays within that region
Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to block requests that contain data from other regions
Store all data in S3 with bucket policies restricting access to the specific region
questions.explanation: Using Bedrock in the required region with cross-region inference disabled is correct for data residency compliance. When cross-region inference is disabled, all model invocations are processed in the specified region, ensuring data does not leave that region. Enabling cross-region inference (option A) would route requests to other regions, violating data residency requirements. Guardrails (option C) apply content filters, not geographic data routing controls. S3 bucket policies (option D) control access to stored data but do not prevent Bedrock from processing data in other regions.

questions.question: A company is implementing governance for their AI systems and wants to track the lineage of their ML models — understanding what training data was used, which preprocessing steps were applied, and which model version is deployed in production. Which AWS service provides ML lineage tracking?
options: AWS CloudTrail to log all SageMaker API calls related to model training and deployment
Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking, which automatically records the relationships between training data, processing jobs, training jobs, models, and endpoints
AWS Config to track configuration changes to SageMaker resources
Amazon SageMaker Experiments to track training runs and hyperparameters
questions.explanation: Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking is correct — it automatically creates a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of the relationships between artifacts (datasets, models), actions (training, processing), and contexts (experiments, endpoints). This provides complete traceability from raw data to deployed model. CloudTrail (option A) logs API calls but does not create semantic lineage relationships between ML artifacts. AWS Config (option C) tracks resource configuration changes but not ML artifact relationships. SageMaker Experiments (option D) tracks training runs and metrics but does not provide the full lineage graph from data to deployment.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement network security so that all traffic between their VPC and the Bedrock API never traverses the public internet. Which AWS networking feature achieves this?
options: AWS Direct Connect to establish a private connection from on-premises to AWS
Amazon VPC interface endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock, routing API traffic through the VPC without internet exposure
AWS WAF to filter and secure traffic to the Bedrock API endpoint
Amazon CloudFront to cache and secure Bedrock API responses
questions.explanation: A VPC interface endpoint (PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock is correct — it creates a private endpoint in the VPC that routes Bedrock API traffic through the AWS private network without traversing the public internet. This is essential for security-sensitive workloads. Direct Connect (option A) provides private connectivity from on-premises to AWS but does not address VPC-to-Bedrock traffic routing. AWS WAF (option C) filters HTTP traffic for security threats but does not change the network path. CloudFront (option D) is a CDN for content delivery, not for securing API traffic routing.

questions.question: A company is implementing a governance framework for their generative AI applications. They want to ensure all AI-generated content can be traced back to the specific model version, prompt, and user that generated it. Which combination of AWS services supports this auditability requirement?
options: Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to capture prompts and responses, combined with AWS CloudTrail to log who made each API call and when
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to track model outputs over time
AWS Config to record configuration changes to Bedrock resources
Amazon CloudWatch metrics to measure model invocation counts per user
questions.explanation: Bedrock model invocation logging combined with CloudTrail is correct for complete auditability. Invocation logging captures the full prompt and response content (what was generated). CloudTrail captures the API call metadata (who made the call, which IAM principal, timestamp, source IP). Together they provide complete traceability: who generated what content, using which model, at what time. SageMaker Model Monitor (option B) monitors for drift in production but does not log individual invocations. AWS Config (option C) tracks resource configuration changes, not content generation. CloudWatch metrics (option D) provide aggregate counts but not per-invocation content.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and wants to test their guardrail configuration before deploying it to production. They want to verify that the guardrail correctly blocks specific harmful content without affecting legitimate requests. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails feature supports this testing?
options: Deploy the guardrail to a test endpoint and manually test with sample prompts
Use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails ApplyGuardrail API to test the guardrail against sample inputs without invoking a foundation model
Use Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluation to run automated tests against the guardrail
Enable guardrail logging and review CloudWatch logs after testing with real traffic
questions.explanation: The ApplyGuardrail API is correct for testing guardrail configurations. It applies the guardrail to a provided input or output without invoking a foundation model, allowing you to test whether specific content is blocked or allowed. This is faster and cheaper than testing with full model invocations. Manual testing with a test endpoint (option A) requires a full model invocation for each test. Model Evaluation (option C) runs batch evaluations but is not designed for guardrail-specific testing. CloudWatch logs after real traffic (option D) tests in production, which is risky — you want to validate before deployment.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to ensure that their foundation model does not generate responses containing their customers' credit card numbers or social security numbers. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails feature should be configured?
options: Content filters set to block harmful content categories
Denied topics configured to block financial and personal information topics
Word filters to block specific numeric patterns
Sensitive information filters configured to detect and redact PII types including credit card numbers and SSNs
questions.explanation: Sensitive information filters are correct — they are specifically designed to detect and handle PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in model inputs and outputs. You can configure them to detect specific PII types (credit card numbers, SSNs, phone numbers, email addresses, etc.) and choose to block, mask, or anonymize them. Content filters (option A) block harmful content categories (hate speech, violence, etc.), not PII. Denied topics (option B) block discussion of specific subjects, not specific data patterns. Word filters (option C) block specific words or phrases but are not designed for pattern-based PII detection like credit card number formats.

questions.question: A company is implementing a compliance framework for their AI systems and needs to demonstrate to auditors that their AI models meet specific regulatory requirements. Which AWS service helps collect evidence and generate audit-ready reports for AI compliance?
options: AWS Audit Manager, which continuously collects evidence from AWS services and maps it to compliance frameworks, generating audit-ready reports
Amazon SageMaker Model Cards to document model compliance characteristics
AWS Config to record all configuration changes to AI resources
AWS CloudTrail to provide a complete audit log of all AI-related API calls
questions.explanation: AWS Audit Manager is correct for generating audit-ready compliance reports. It continuously collects evidence from AWS services (CloudTrail, Config, Security Hub, etc.) and maps it to compliance frameworks (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, etc.). It generates pre-built reports that auditors can review. SageMaker Model Cards (option B) document model characteristics but are not an audit evidence collection tool. AWS Config (option C) records configuration changes and is a data source for Audit Manager, but does not generate compliance reports. CloudTrail (option D) provides API audit logs and is also a data source for Audit Manager, but does not generate compliance framework reports.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement data governance for their AI pipeline. They need to ensure that sensitive customer data used for fine-tuning is encrypted, access-controlled, and its usage is tracked. Which combination of AWS services addresses these requirements?
options: Store fine-tuning data in S3 with server-side encryption, use IAM policies to control access, and enable S3 server access logging and CloudTrail data events to track access
Store fine-tuning data in Amazon RDS with encryption enabled and use VPC security groups for access control
Use Amazon Macie to automatically encrypt and access-control sensitive data in S3
Store fine-tuning data in AWS Secrets Manager to ensure it is encrypted and access-controlled
questions.explanation: S3 with encryption, IAM policies, and access logging is the correct combination. S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) encrypts data at rest. IAM policies control which principals can access the fine-tuning data. S3 server access logging and CloudTrail data events track every access to the data, providing the audit trail. Amazon RDS (option B) is a relational database, not appropriate for storing ML training files. Amazon Macie (option C) discovers and classifies sensitive data in S3 but does not encrypt or access-control it — it is a discovery tool. AWS Secrets Manager (option D) stores secrets (API keys, passwords), not large training datasets.

questions.question: A company is deploying a generative AI application and wants to implement the principle of least privilege for their Amazon Bedrock usage. The application should only be able to invoke specific models and access specific Knowledge Bases. Which IAM policy structure achieves this?
options: Attach the AWS managed policy AmazonBedrockFullAccess to the application role
Create a custom IAM policy with Allow statements for bedrock:InvokeModel on specific model ARNs and bedrock:Retrieve on specific Knowledge Base ARNs
Use resource-based policies on the Bedrock models to allow access from the application role
Use AWS Organizations SCPs to restrict Bedrock access at the account level
questions.explanation: A custom IAM policy with specific resource ARNs is correct for least privilege. The policy allows bedrock:InvokeModel only on the specific model ARNs the application needs, and bedrock:Retrieve only on the specific Knowledge Base ARNs. This prevents the application from accessing other models or knowledge bases. AmazonBedrockFullAccess (option A) grants access to all Bedrock resources and actions — the opposite of least privilege. Resource-based policies on Bedrock models (option C) do not exist — Bedrock uses identity-based IAM policies. SCPs (option D) restrict what accounts can do but are not the right tool for application-level least privilege.

questions.question: A company is using Amazon Bedrock and wants to implement a data governance strategy that ensures their proprietary training data used for fine-tuning is not used by AWS to train or improve foundation models. Which Amazon Bedrock data privacy commitment addresses this concern?
options: Enable Amazon Bedrock data encryption to prevent AWS from accessing training data
Use a VPC endpoint for Bedrock to ensure data stays within the company's network
Amazon Bedrock does not use customer data (prompts, completions, fine-tuning data) to train or improve AWS foundation models by default — this is a contractual commitment
Sign an AWS Business Associate Agreement (BAA) to prevent data use for model training
questions.explanation: Amazon Bedrock's data privacy commitment is correct — AWS contractually commits that customer data (prompts, responses, fine-tuning data) is not used to train or improve AWS foundation models. This is a fundamental data privacy guarantee of the service. Encryption (option A) protects data from unauthorized access but does not address how AWS uses the data for model training. VPC endpoints (option B) keep network traffic private but do not address data usage policies. A BAA (option D) is for HIPAA compliance covering protected health information — it does not specifically address AI model training data usage.
